title: CO₂ Snow Cleaning of Red Clay and Starch Deposits on Natural Fibre Textiles: Multi-Analytical Material Response Profiles
content: The response of a material to CO₂ snow cleaning is conditional on both the structure of the deposit and the morphology of the textile. To examine these two factors under controlled conditions, six model systems were compared, in which three natural fibre textiles (silk, cotton, and linen) were combined with two representative types of deposit: a particulate red clay deposit, and a gelatinised wheat starch film. Eighteen treated specimens were characterised before the application of the deposit (M0), after application and drying (M1), and after CO₂ snow treatment (M2), which was performed using predefined configurations ranging from 1.5 to 6 bar and from 1 to 4 min. Optical and surface measurements were taken over trajectories at the specimen level (M0–M1–M2). In parallel, attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) provided local spectral characterisation at selected contact sites, while digital and field-emission scanning electron microscopy supplied complementary morphological evidence at different observation scales. The two types of deposit produced distinct response profiles, with visible and chromatic changes predominating in the clay systems and surface-sensitive measurements providing greater differentiation in the starch systems. After treatment, residual colour differences (ΔE*ab) ranged from 6.65 to 34.00 for the red clay specimens and from 0.21 to 2.88 for the starch. At 85°, post-treatment gloss was below the clean textile (M0) value in 16 of the 18 specimens. The two remaining specimens, both from the linen starch group, had M2 readings above M0. The 60° gloss response of the starch systems varied across textiles. Normalised ATR-FTIR band ratios reflected the attenuation of deposit-associated bands at selected contact sites, while the residual material and local surface morphology were examined via microscopy. This integrated analytical approach differentiated between particulate and film-forming deposits, and showed that each textile–deposit system was characterised by a specific combination of optical, surface, spectroscopic, and morphological indicators.
